q.t: How many questions are there in the Life in the UK test, and what are they based on?
q.e: The test consists of 24 questions about important aspects of life in the UK. Questions are based on ALL parts of the handbook. The 24 questions will be different for each person taking the test at that test session.
o: 24 questions, based on all parts of the handbook
45 questions, based on all parts of the handbook
24 questions, based only on the history chapter
12 questions, based on all parts of the handbook

q.t: In which TWO languages, other than English, can special arrangements be made to take the Life in the UK test?
q.e: The Life in the UK test is usually taken in English, although special arrangements can be made if you wish to take it in Welsh or Scottish Gaelic.

q.t: Roughly how many registered Life in the UK test centres are there around the UK?
q.e: You can only take the test at a registered and approved Life in the UK test centre. There are about 60 test centres around the UK. You can only book your test online.

q.t: What must you take with you to the test?
q.e: When booking your test, read the instructions carefully. You will need to take some identification and proof of your address with you to the test. If you don't take these, you will not be able to take the test.
o: Identification and proof of your address

q.t: Which people on work visas normally must pass the Life in the UK test to become permanent residents?
q.e: People here on work visas, including those on Tier 1 and Tier 2 of the points based system, normally must pass the Life in the UK test to become permanent residents.
o: Those on Tier 1 and Tier 2 of the points based system
Only those on Tier 4 student visas
Only those married to a British citizen

q.t: To apply to become a permanent resident or citizen of the UK, what must you be able to do?
q.e: To apply to become a permanent resident or citizen of the UK, you will need to speak and read English, and have a good understanding of life in the UK.
o: Speak and read English, and have a good understanding of life in the UK
Speak Welsh and have lived in the UK for ten years
Own property in the UK and pay income tax
Serve in the armed forces and pass a medical test

q.t: At what level of English are the Life in the UK test questions written?
q.e: The questions are written in a way that requires an understanding of the English language at English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) Entry Level 3, so there is no need to take a separate English language test.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Pass an ESOL course in English with Citizenship. You will need to take this course if your standard of English is below ESOL Entry Level 3. The course will help you to improve your English and learn more about life in the UK.
o: An ESOL course in English with Citizenship is needed if your English is below Entry Level 3
An ESOL course in English with Citizenship is needed only if your English is above Entry Level 3

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
There is a fee for submitting an application for permanent residence, and it differs for the various types of application.
q.e: Once you have passed one of these tests, you can make an application for permanent residence or British citizenship. There is a fee for submitting an application, which is different for the various types of application.

q.t: Which of these is NOT one of the countries that make up the UK?
q.e: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The rest of Ireland is an independent country.

q.t: Which TWO of these are British overseas territories named in the handbook?
q.e: There are also several British overseas territories in other parts of the world, such as St Helena and the Falkland Islands. They are also linked to the UK but are not a part of it.

q.t: Where does the parliament that governs the whole UK sit?
q.e: The UK is governed by the parliament sitting in Westminster. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland also have parliaments or assemblies of their own, with devolved powers in defined areas.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: There are also several islands which are closely linked with the UK but are not part of it: the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. These have their own governments and are called 'Crown dependencies'.
o: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man have their own governments
The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are governed from Westminster

q.t: Which body would you contact to register to vote?
q.e: To be able to vote in a parliamentary, local or European election, you must have your name on the electoral register. If you are eligible to vote, you can register by contacting your local council electoral registration office.
o: Your local council electoral registration office

q.t: When is the electoral register updated each year?
q.e: The electoral register is updated every year in September or October. An electoral registration form is sent to every household and this has to be completed and returned with the names of everyone who is resident in the household and eligible to vote.

q.t: What is different about voter registration in Northern Ireland?
q.e: In Northern Ireland a different system operates. This is called 'individual registration' and all those entitled to vote must complete their own registration form. Once registered, people stay on the register provided their personal details do not change.
o: Individual registration, where everyone completes their own form
Registration is done by the local police

q.t: At what times are polling stations open on election day?
q.e: People vote in elections at places called polling stations, or polling places in Scotland. On election day, the polling station or place will be open from 7.00 am until 10.00 pm.

q.t: What must voters in Northern Ireland show at the polling station?
q.e: When you arrive at the polling station, the staff will ask for your name and address. In Northern Ireland you will also have to show photographic identification.

q.t: Which TWO groups of resident citizens can vote in ALL public elections in the UK?
q.e: Adult citizens of the UK, and citizens of the Commonwealth and the Irish Republic who are resident in the UK, can vote in all public elections. Adult citizens of other EU states who are resident in the UK can vote in all elections except General Elections.
o: Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK
Irish Republic citizens resident in the UK
EU citizens resident in the UK

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Adult citizens of other EU states who are resident in the UK can vote in all elections except General Elections. Adult citizens of the UK, and citizens of the Commonwealth and the Irish Republic who are resident in the UK, can vote in all public elections.
o: Resident EU citizens can vote in all elections except General Elections
Resident EU citizens can vote in all elections including General Elections

q.t: Which TWO of these groups cannot stand for public office?
q.e: Most citizens of the UK, the Irish Republic or the Commonwealth aged 18 or over can stand for public office. There are some exceptions, including members of the armed forces, civil servants, and people found guilty of certain criminal offences.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Members of the House of Lords may stand for election to the House of Commons.
q.e: Members of the House of Lords may not stand for election to the House of Commons but are eligible for all other public offices.

q.t: What can you do if it is difficult for you to get to a polling station?
q.e: If it is difficult for you to get to a polling station or polling place, you can register for a postal ballot. Your ballot paper will be sent to your home before the election. You then fill it in and post it back.
o: Ask a neighbour to vote on your behalf
Send your poll card to the council

q.t: How much does it cost to enter the public galleries of the Palace of Westminster?
q.e: The public can listen to debates in the Palace of Westminster from public galleries in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords. You can write to your local MP in advance to ask for tickets or you can queue on the day at the public entrance. Entrance is free.
o: £5 for the Commons and £5 for the Lords
It is free only for UK citizens
